   A property is within the carve-out only where the turf in question lies inside the recorded boundary of an
   individually-owned single-family residential lot. Turf lying outside those boundaries — even by inches, and
   even where the adjacent lot owner mows it — is not within the carve-out. Developers, landscape architects, and
   HOA managers are cautioned that the presence of a single-family residential zoning designation on the
   underlying parcel does not confer the carve-out on common-area turf within that parcel; the operative
   distinction is the lot line, not the zoning district.

   3. Functional Turf Categories
   Turf that lies outside the single-family residential carve-out is subject to the prohibition unless it qualifies under
   one of the functional categories set out below. Each category has a specific qualifying test. Turf that does not
   satisfy the test for one of these categories is nonfunctional turf and must be converted on or before the deadline.

   3.1 Playground Turf
   Definition. Grass located within a designated play area containing playground amenities including slides,
   swings, and climbing structures, on homeowner association owned or managed common-area property.
   Qualifying test. All of the following must be present:

   1. The turf lies within a designated play area — that is, an area drawn on approved landscape plans, or
         established on the ground by fencing, borders, or other physical delineation, and identified as a play area
         intended for use by children.

   2. The designated play area contains installed and operable playground amenities of the character enumerated
         above — specifically, slides, swings, and climbing structures. A designated play area lacking installed
         playground amenities does not qualify as playground turf, regardless of the sign or plan label attached to
         the area.

   3. The turf lies on property owned or managed by a homeowner association, or by a comparable body
         responsible for the common-area landscape.
   Turf lying outside the boundary of the designated play area — even in the same park parcel, and even if
   visually continuous with the qualifying turf — does not fall within this category and must be classified
   independently.

   3.2 Athletic Field Turf
   Definition. A contiguous turf area of not less than 1,500 contiguous square feet with no dimension less than
   30 feet, used for organized athletic activity.
   Qualifying test. All of the following must be present:
   1. The turf area is contiguous — i.e., forming a single, connected surface uninterrupted by pavement, planter,
         structure, or non-turf ground cover — and measures at least 1,500 square feet in aggregate area.

   2. The shortest dimension of that contiguous area, measured perpendicular to its longest dimension, is not
         less than 30 feet.

   3. The area is used, or is dedicated to be used, for organized athletic activity — organized team sports,
         physical education, formal recreation league play, or similar use. General passive lawn use, decorative
         lawn, and informal recreation do not satisfy this element.
   A grass area meeting the geometric thresholds but lacking a documented athletic use does not qualify.
   Conversely, a grass area used for organized athletic activity that fails either the 1,500-square-foot minimum or
   the 30-foot minimum dimension does not qualify.

   3.3 Pet Relief Turf (Limited)
   Turf provided as a pet-relief area on multi-family residential, hotel, or comparable properties may qualify as
   functional in limited circumstances. Where allowed, pet-relief turf is capped at a modest area per property, must
   be enclosed, must be identified by signage, and must be reasonably necessary in light of the character of the
   property served. Pet-relief turf on HOA common area serving single-family residential subdivisions is generally
   not recognized under this category and should not be relied on to justify continued irrigation of common-area
   lawn.

   3.4 Special-Use Turf by Application
   Turf that serves a demonstrable functional purpose not captured by the categories above — for example,
   cemetery lawn, historic-district lawn, or grass specified by an accessibility program — may be recognized as
   functional on a case-by-case basis by written application to SNWA. Applications shall document the intended
   use, the physical and administrative measures that confine the turf to that use, and the reason the turf cannot be

   4. Waiver and Alternative Compliance
   Waiver of the removal requirement is available in narrow circumstances, and only where the application
   demonstrates that the turf in question substantially complies with the functional turf definition for one of the
   categories in Section 3. A waiver application shall include:

   •   A dimensioned exhibit showing the turf area and the elements relied upon to establish functional character
       (for playground turf, the boundary of the designated play area and the location and description of installed
       playground amenities; for athletic field turf, the contiguous area with dimensions and evidence of organized
       use);
   •   A written statement identifying the functional category asserted and addressing each element of that
       category's qualifying test;

   •   A declaration by the property owner or its authorized agent that the exhibit and statement are true and that
       the functional use will be maintained after the compliance deadline.
   Waiver applications will be reviewed against the qualifying test for the category asserted. A waiver is not
   available for turf that does not meet a functional category. In particular:

   •   A designated play area that does not contain installed playground amenities cannot be waived under Section
       3.1 by promising future amenities; installation must be complete on or before the deadline.

   •   A lawn intended for passive use, decorative purpose, aesthetic frontage, or general open space cannot be
       waived under Section 3.2 by asserting occasional recreational use; the organized-athletic-activity element is
       a use test, not an aspiration.

   •   The presence of expense, hardship, or aesthetic preference is not, standing alone, a ground for waiver.
   Alternative compliance measures — including phased conversion schedules, in-lieu turf reduction at other
   properties in common ownership, and coordination with member-agency incentive programs — are available on
   application and may be combined with, but do not substitute for, the qualifying test.

   5. Enforcement
   On and after 12/31/2026, nonfunctional turf on a property subject to the prohibition constitutes a continuing
   violation. SNWA and its member agencies will exercise the following enforcement mechanisms, singly or in
   combination:

   1. Notice of Violation. A written notice identifying the property, the noncompliant turf area, and a cure
         period.

   2. Excess-Use Water Rates. Application of the member agency's excess-use rate schedule to the account
         serving the property, retroactive to the deadline where the violation is continuing.

   3. Water Waste Fees. Assessment of water waste fees under the member agency's schedule for continued
         irrigation of nonfunctional turf.

   4. Flow Restriction and Service Discontinuation. In cases of protracted noncompliance, installation of a
         flow restrictor on the service and, ultimately, discontinuation of water service in accordance with the
         member agency's service rules and Nevada law.

   Appendix A — Glossary
      Contiguous. Forming a single, connected turf surface, uninterrupted by pavement, planter, structure, or

      Designated play area. An area drawn on approved landscape plans as a play area, or established on the
      ground by fencing, borders, or comparable physical delineation, and intended for use by children.
      Functional turf. Turf that satisfies the qualifying test for one of the categories set out in Section 3.
      Homeowner association (HOA). A nonprofit corporation or unincorporated association organized under
      the governing documents of a common-interest community and vested with authority to own or manage
      common areas.
      Nonfunctional turf. Turf that does not satisfy the qualifying test for a functional category and does not lie
      within the single-family residential carve-out.
      Playground amenities. Installed play equipment intended for use by children, including slides, swings, and
      climbing structures.
      Single-family residential lot. An individually-owned parcel improved or intended to be improved with a
      single-family dwelling, the boundary of which is recorded on a final subdivision map or parcel map.

Dear Garrett,

Thank you for the update at last week’s coordination call and for keeping our office in the loop as the Phase
3 improvement plans and final map move through their current review cycle. The Phase 1/2 Board and the
homeowners we work with share Callaway’s interest in a smooth recordation, and this letter is offered in
that spirit — as an early flag on a couple of items the Board would like to have addressed before Phase 3
crosses the counter, so that questions from the community do not surface at a less convenient moment.

Nonfunctional turf conversion — Phase 1/2 common areas. The Board reviewed the Southern Nevada
Water Authority nonfunctional turf compliance materials at its October regular meeting and has taken
counsel from our office and from a landscape contractor on what the 12/31/2026 deadline means for the
association. Our understanding, and the advice we have been given, is that any turf conversion required in
the existing Phase 1/2 common areas — parcels the association owns and maintains — is a cost that falls to
the association rather than to the developer, and the Board has begun budgeting on that basis. Current
pricing we have collected from two local contractors for turf-to-desert conversion in park settings runs on
the order of $2.85 per square foot, inclusive of removal, soil prep, drip retrofit, decomposed granite, and a
modest planting palette. Even the areas the Board expects to keep as functional playground turf still leave a
scope that, when combined with adjacent landscape refresh the community has been discussing, is projected
to reach into the tens of thousands of dollars for the association in the next reserve cycle. The Board is
prepared to absorb its share of that obligation. It has, however, asked me to make sure the developer’s team
is aware that the community is watching how the Phase 3 landscape reads against the same standard.

Phase 3 park — playground amenities. The Board’s second and more forward-looking question concerns
the Phase 3 park. On the current landscape sheets circulated at the September coordination meeting, the
Phase 3 park parcel reads to us as a turfed lawn without the play equipment the Phase 1/2 park carries. The
Phase 1/2 park was built with slides, swings, and climbing structures inside a bordered play area, and in
every homeowner survey we have run since 2024 that playground has come up as one of the two or three
most-used common-area amenities in the community — ahead of the trail loop and the ramada, and
comparable to the pool. Families with children moved to Desert Sage Ranch in part because of it.

We are asking, plainly, whether the Phase 3 park will include the same playground amenities — slides,
swings, and climbing structures within a designated play area — as the Phase 1/2 park. The Board would
like to be able to tell homeowners that the answer is yes. If the current design does not carry those amenities
 forward, the Board would appreciate the opportunity to sit down with your landscape architect and Mr.
Braddock’s team before the resubmittal is finalized, to understand the reasoning and to discuss whether there
is room to reintroduce them. We recognize that the two questions above are related in ways that the Board
does not need to spell out here; the design team will see them, and we trust the design team to weigh them.

Enterprise Town Advisory Board — 11/18/2026. In the interest of transparency, and so this does not come
as a surprise: a group of Phase 1/2 homeowners has organized to attend the Enterprise Town Advisory Board
meeting on 11/18/2026 and to address the Phase 3 park treatment during public comment. They intend to
speak respectfully and to focus on the amenity question rather than on personalities or on Callaway’s
broader entitlement, but they will speak, and the local paper occasionally covers TAB comment. The Board
has not endorsed any particular position for the homeowners to take; it has, however, declined to discourage
them from attending. I mention it now, rather than the week before, so that the Callaway team and Sundial
have time to consider whether an outreach conversation ahead of that meeting would be useful.

Offer to coordinate. Our office is available to host a joint working session at the Sagebrook offices in the
next two to three weeks, at whatever time suits Callaway and Sundial, with the Phase 1/2 Board president
and our landscape committee chair present. If it would help, I can also circulate the homeowner survey
results and the two contractor quotes referenced above in advance of any such meeting, so that the numbers
we are working from are in front of everyone. Please let me know how you would like to proceed. I remain
the point of contact for the association on this matter and am reachable at the direct line and email below.

Thank you again for your continued attention to the community as Desert Sage Ranch completes its final
phase. The Board’s goal, and mine, is a Phase 3 that feels of a piece with what is already built — for the new
homeowners as well as for the ones already here.

Sincerely,


Ruthann Meeker

Callaway Land Partners was invited but did not attend; Max Braddock represented applicant-side coordination.
2. Purpose
Pre-application discussion of the Desert Sage Ranch Phase 3 improvement plan and final map resubmittal package under the current code cycle. Objective was to align the design team and County reviewers on submittal composition, review path, and any threshold issues that ought to be flagged before intake, so the package can move through Public Works plan check on the first submittal without a routing surprise.
Phase 3 is the final 40.0 acres (60 half-acre lots) of the 140-acre subdivision entitled under Tentative Map TM-22-500041 (approved 03/14/2022). Phases 1 and 2 are built and occupied; the first final map in the series was recorded in 2024.
3. Topics Discussed
3.1 Submittal package composition and application numbers. Max walked through the intended package. County has already issued application numbers on the intake pre-check:
Improvement Plans: IP-26-100288
Final Map: FM-26-100290
Package as contemplated for first submittal:
Improvement plan set (grading, drainage, streets, wet/dry utility composite) — Sundial
Landscape and irrigation set — Ocotillo Landscape Studio
Final Map (three-sheet, second in the TM-22-500041 series) — Sundial Survey
Supporting reports: updated drainage narrative referencing the approved master drainage study; geotechnical addendum; traffic memo confirming trip generation is unchanged from tentative-map assumptions
Title report and closure package — Callaway to procure through Silver Butte Title & Escrow
Agency will-serve / capacity confirmations from LVVWD and CCWRD (see 3.5)
Dale Yeoman confirmed the two application numbers above are the correct references and should appear on the title block and cover sheets of every submitted sheet. He asked that IP-26-100288 be cited on the drainage narrative title page as well.
3.2 Drainage — master study governs. Priya summarized the drainage approach: Phase 3 drains to the detention basin sized under the approved master drainage study for the subdivision. Detention allocation for Phase 3 was fixed in that study; there are no departures anticipated in the resubmittal.
Dale confirmed that so long as the Phase 3 improvement plans match the volumes and outfall configuration in the district-approved master drainage study, no fresh hydrology submittal to Regional Flood Control is required — a narrative-level reconciliation in the drainage report is sufficient. He noted plan check will still verify the basin geometry against the study.
Priya to include a reconciliation table (basin volume as built into Phase 1/2, allocations for Phase 3, and headroom) in the drainage narrative.
3.3 Landscape — significant-change threshold. Bea Cortland summarized the landscape approach: streetscape palette carried forward from the approved 2022 Phase 1/2 palette (desert planting throughout streetscapes; turf confined to the HOA common-area park). Species list is substantially the same as Phase 1/2. Some substitutions in the shrub layer may be proposed as availability has shifted since 2022.
Odette Marchetti raised that any landscape changes from the approved 2022 palette may require review beyond staff level depending on extent — the significant-change threshold has to be evaluated on the actual proposed change. She referenced condition 14 of the tentative map approval letter, which contemplates design review as a public hearing before the Town Advisory Board and Planning Commission for significant changes to approved plans, including landscape and streetscape treatments in common areas.
Discussion did not resolve where the significant-change threshold sits for this project. Odette noted the evaluation is fact-specific and that the design team should provide a red-line comparison of the proposed Phase 3 palette against the 2022 approved palette so Planning can make that call once the actual proposed change is on paper. Bea agreed to prepare that comparison as part of the landscape resubmittal.
No commitment was made at the meeting as to whether the resubmittal will or will not trigger design review. The point was flagged for the team's awareness; a written determination from Planning would follow the submittal.
3.4 Fire access. Lt. Salazar (attending for Capt. Roark) noted that the CCFD review will focus on the permanent buildout access configuration for Phase 3. The temporary secondary access accepted at Phase 2 buildout was approved as a temporary condition pending Phase 3 development, and Phase 3 improvement plans need to show the permanent second point of access consistent with the tentative map. Any deviation from what was shown on TM-22-500041 should be pre-coordinated with Capt. Roark before submittal.
Sundial to circulate the current Phase 3 access layout to CCFD in advance of the formal submittal for informal review; the substantive determination on the permanent buildout condition will come from CCFD through the plan check letter.
3.5 Utilities. K. Odhiambo confirmed that separate confirmations from Las Vegas Valley Water District (LVVWD) and Clark County Water Reclamation District (CCWRD) will be needed for the resubmittal package. These are separate agency confirmations obtained by the applicant/engineer directly with each district; the County does not procure them.
Noted for the record; no further discussion.
3.6 SWPPP / grading permit sequencing. Priya asked about sequencing between improvement plan approval and the grading permit / SWPPP. Dale confirmed the standard sequence:
Improvement plans routed and approved (IP-26-100288)
NDEP Bureau of Water Pollution Control NOI filed by contractor; SWPPP prepared under NPDES general construction permit
Grading permit application submitted to Public Works with the SWPPP and approved improvement plans referenced
Grading permit issued once bonds/estimate are posted through Callaway
The grading permit cannot issue ahead of improvement plan approval. Dale mentioned that Callaway will need to have the surety and cost estimate lined up on the Public Works side before grading permit issuance, but that this is not a first-submittal item.
4. Agreed Submittal Route
The resubmittal will be routed through Clark County Public Works, Development Review, with Comprehensive Planning coordination on the landscape and final map conditions. Dale Yeoman is the assigned civil plans examiner (Public Works). Odette Marchetti is the point of contact on the Comprehensive Planning side for the tentative map conditions carry-forward and the significant-change evaluation.
Public Works will circulate the improvement plans internally to CCFD and Landscape review. Applicant is responsible for obtaining LVVWD and CCWRD confirmations separately (see 3.5) and including them in the submittal package.
Formal intake will be at the Public Works counter under application numbers IP-26-100288 (improvement plans) and FM-26-100290 (final map).

            print(' | '.join(cells)); words += sum(len(c.split()) for c in cells)
        print('---')
print('\nWORDS:', words)
EOF

SUNDIAL ENGINEERING & SURVEY
4720 South Rainbow Boulevard, Suite 210  ·  Las Vegas, Nevada 89103  ·  (702) 555-0142  ·  NV COA #C-3874
MEMORANDUM
TO: | Garrett Nokes, Vice President, Land Development — Callaway Land Partners
FROM: | Max Braddock, Project Manager — Sundial Engineering & Survey
DATE: | October 31, 2026
RE: | Desert Sage Ranch Phase 3 — County comment L-4 (street frontage trees) and the 11/30/2026 resubmittal / IP-26-100288  ·  FM-26-100290  ·  TM-22-500041  ·  Job No. 2201-03
CC: | Lee Chastain (Callaway); Bea Cortland, PLA (Ocotillo Landscape Studio); Priya Sarwal, EIT; Jonathan R. Kessler, PE; File 2201-03
---
1.  Bottom line
Not yet. The L-4 drafting fits inside 11/30. What is not settled are four items outside the drafting, and they decide whether the L-4 response survives second-round review. They need to close by Friday, November 13. If they do, I will commit to 11/30 for L-4, and I recommend going in earlier. If Comprehensive Planning treats the revision as a “significant change” under TM Condition 14, no resubmittal date protects the 12/18 recordation.
This is not a clerical redline. Yeoman’s 10/09 letter requires 208 street trees (one per 20 lf on 4,160 lf). Sheet L-2 shows 58. That means 150 more trees placed clear of sight triangles and easements, and the plant schedule, irrigation demand, water budget and bond estimate all change with them. Our notes already say trees are at 20 ft on center, but the count works out to about one tree per 72 ft. A redline that changes only the count would draw the same comment again, and there is no time for a third round. (Comment L-4 is answered on Sheets L-1 and L-2. Sheet L-4 is the entry monument.)
2.  What has to happen first
# | What has to happen | Why it controls the date | Owner | Need by
1 | Planning’s written determination that the street-tree revision is not a “significant change” under TM Condition 14. | If it is, a TAB and Planning Commission hearing must come before any staff approval. The 11/18 TAB filing cutoff (10/28) has passed. The next TAB is 12/16, and the Commission follows it, past 12/18 (Section 3.1). | Braddock to O. Marchetti; Ocotillo prepares red-line comparison | Ask Mon 11/02; answer by Fri 11/13
2 | Callaway decision on the Parcel A park program. | The revised irrigation demand that L-4 requires runs from 2.3 to 4.2 ac-ft/yr, depending on the park (Section 3.2). | Callaway (Nokes), with counsel | Fri 11/06
3 | Placement check of all 208 trees on an updated survey base. | At 20 ft o.c. there is no slack. Trees cannot go in sight triangles, or in easements without written utility consent. If the count does not fit, the fixes take longer than 11/30 allows (Section 3.3). | Survey (easement base); Ocotillo (layout); Sarwal (back-check) | Tue 11/10
4 | Frontage basis confirmed before the count is locked. | The County will check our 4,160 lf against the map. It does not reconcile to the civil boundary (Section 3.4). | Halvorsen (certify lengths); Braddock (confirm with Yeoman) | Fri 11/06; Yeoman by 11/10
---
3.  Why each item controls the date
3.1  Condition 14: get Planning’s answer before we submit. 
Condition 14 requires a design-review public hearing before the Enterprise TAB and the Planning Commission, prior to staff-level action, for any significant change to approved plans, “including but not limited to landscape and streetscape treatments in common areas.” At the 06/22 pre-app, Odette Marchetti called that threshold fact-specific. She asked for a red-line comparison against the 2022 approved palette and said Planning’s determination would follow the submittal. Advisory A-3 in Yeoman’s letter repeats the point. I know you want nothing that adds process or TAB time. A staff determination letter is how we avoid both. Without one, Planning can raise Condition 14 in December, with no time left to answer. (The 12/16 TAB filing cutoff is 11/25. After that, the next meeting is in January 2027.)
Our position is strong if we keep it narrow. The Phase 1/2 landscape that Planning approved in 2022 already calls for one tree per 20 lf at 20 ft on center, using the species we carry (Desert Willow, Palo Verde, Mesquite). Bringing Phase 3 up to that standard matches the approved character, and Condition 25 requires it anyway. To protect that position:
Send Planning a streetscape-only red-line comparison next week.
Stay within the 2022 species palette and section design. That rules out cutting the count by switching to large-canopy species at one per 30 lf (about 140 trees).
Keep the street trees separate from the park palette changes Ocotillo raised on 10/30. Those carry the real Condition 14 risk. Phase 1/2 homeowners plan to speak about the park at the 11/18 TAB, so expect Planning to read this resubmittal closely.
3.2  The irrigation number cannot be finalized until the park is decided. 
L-4 requires a revised annual irrigation demand, which is one total for all Phase 3 landscape. The park lawn accounts for 2.32 of today’s 3.28 ac-ft/yr. Using Ocotillo’s own rates:
Park program | Street trees | Turf | Drip | Trees (all) | Total ac-ft/yr
As submitted 08/21 (18,400 sf lawn) | 58 | 2.32 | 0.51 | 0.45 | 3.28
L-4 trees added; lawn kept as drawn | 208 | 2.32 | 0.51 | 1.37 | 4.20
L-4 trees; 4,200 sf play-area turf (Phase 1/2 model), rest drip | 208 | 0.53 | 0.84 | 1.37 | 2.74
L-4 trees; all turf converted to drip | 208 | — | 0.93 | 1.37 | 2.30
---
Rates per Ocotillo’s 08/15/2026 worksheet: spray turf 5.5 ft/yr; drip 1.0 ft/yr; 2,000 gal/tree/yr. Tree totals include 6 entry and 10 park trees. Conversion rows assume the converted area is fully drip-planted (upper bound).
So there is no single number to put “behind” the tree count until the park is set. On the turf question, three sources point the same way:
Yeoman’s comment L-3 asks for functional-turf classification of all common-area turf.
SNWA Bulletin WRC-2024-07 says the single-family carve-out is lot-based. HOA park parcels are covered whatever the zoning.
The County’s March 2025 canopy guidance expects HOA park turf to meet a functional (playground or athletic) definition. Since the VE cut, the 18,400 sf lawn has no play equipment.
This is a legal question, and I am not offering an opinion on it. Please ask Adrienne Vogel to address the bulletin’s lot-based language directly, because a demand figure built on the lawn as drawn is likely to come back. A Phase 1/2-style play area comes closest to the approved park and to the HOA’s request, but it adds cost. That decision is yours, under L-2/L-3. If the lawn stays, demand rises 28%. We should then confirm that the 07/22/2026 LVVWD will-serve still covers it, since it covers the common-area demand “indicated in the developer’s submittal.”
3.3  The 150 added trees have to physically fit. 
At 20 ft on center, 4,160 lf holds exactly 208 trees. Every station lost to a sight triangle, hydrant, inlet or easement has to be made up elsewhere on the same frontage.
TM Condition 6 requires sight-visibility triangles on the landscape plans at every intersection and driveway. The traffic study requires one at Desert Sage Pkwy./Windmill Ln.
Our own notes (L-1 Note 12; L-2) bar trees in utility easements without written utility consent. The easements include:
– NV Energy’s easement over the westerly 10 ft, on the Rainbow side (title exception 7);
– the 10-ft P.U.E. across all lot frontages on our final map;
– joint-trench lateral JT-B along the east side of Desert Sage Pkwy.;
– an unplotted 1989 LVVWD transmission easement (exception 8); and
– the Southwest Gas regulator station on Rainbow.
Our Phase 3 CAD base, which Ocotillo draws on, still carries easements from the 2022 tentative-map exhibit. That exhibit omits easements created by later maps, so the survey base update (M-2/M-4) comes first. The landscape sheets also need re-basing on the civil set. Sheet L-4 places the entry at Rainbow Blvd., but FA-1 and the traffic study show the only permanent connection at Desert Sage Pkwy./Windmill Ln.
If the count will not fit, there are two remedies: written consent from each easement holder (NV Energy, Southwest Gas, CenturyLink, Cox, and LVVWD where applicable), or a discretionary Alternative Standards approval from Planning under sec. 30.64.050. Neither can happen by 11/30. Ocotillo will also run the County’s 30% shade-coverage check now. L-4 does not ask for it, but staff apply it, and a shortfall would mean more or larger trees.
3.4  Confirm the frontage before we lock the count. 
The County’s 208 is our own 4,160 lf divided by 20, and its guidance says staff verify footage against the map along each property line. On our civil control, Rainbow scales at about 665 ft (we counted 420) and Windmill at about 2,640 ft (we counted 2,560). Measured that way, about 225 trees are required. We also excluded interior-street frontage as “owner-planted.” Callaway’s recorded CC&Rs, however, contemplate HOA streetscape with street trees along Phase 3 interior streets (Exhibit B, Parcel S-4). If staff count those streets, the requirement rises by several hundred trees. Marcus Halvorsen will certify the lengths from the map geometry. I will then put our basis and exclusions to Yeoman and confirm in writing; his letter invites that call. Better to settle this now than in round two.
4.  Why 11/30 is the outside date, not the target
The deadline behind 12/18. NRS 278.360, as quoted in the TM approval, gives each successive final map two years from the previous map’s recording. Phases 1–2 recorded 12/23/2024, so our working deadline is 12/23/2026. On 10/16 Planning asked for the recording particulars in writing before it confirms on letterhead, and I am sending them Monday. Please disregard the 2028 date in the title officer’s 10/26 email. It applies the first-map clock to a successive map. Planning’s 12/30/2024 letter says an extension can be sought only after a deadline has passed, and granting it is discretionary.
The review clock. An 11/30 resubmittal leaves the County 14 business days to 12/18. Yeoman quotes 20 for second round (ending 12/29), and Phase 2’s second round took 37 calendar days. 11/18 is the last date that gives the County its standard 20 days.
Plan. Lock the landscape set on 11/13 and finish QC by 11/18. The tracker’s 11/22 internal target falls on a Sunday and leaves about three working days for QC around Thanksgiving. I will also ask Yeoman for priority review given the statutory date.
5.  Cost and bond
150 added 24-inch box trees ($485, County schedule item 7.09) plus drip assemblies ($12.50, item 7.42) add $74,625. That moves the engineer’s estimate from $5,357,000 to about $5,432,000. Please hold the $5,357,000 figure with the surety broker. A re-sealed Rev. 1 goes in with the resubmittal, as Advisory A-6 asks. The park decision will move the figure again. The estimate carries the lawn as “functional turf,” and the County schedule does not allow nonfunctional turf to be bonded.
6.  What I need from you
1.  Your OK to request Planning’s written Condition 14 determination, by Monday 11/02. This is a staff letter, not a TAB item.
2.  Direction on the Parcel A park program by Friday 11/06.
3.  Agreement that L-4 stays within the 2022 species palette and goes in separately from any park redesign.
4.  Hold the bond figure until Rev. 1 is issued.
My commitment: if the Section 2 items close by 11/13, Sundial will deliver the L-4 response for an 11/30 resubmittal, and earlier if the rest of the package is ready. The response will include:
revised Sheets L-1 and L-2, with every tree, sight triangle and easement plotted;
the frontage tabulation and the shade-coverage exhibit;
a reconciled irrigation worksheet, water budget and planting tabulation;
the revised estimate; and
all L-sheets sealed.
This memo covers L-4 only. The package date also depends on items outside landscape. The most immediate are the CCWRD sewer capacity confirmation (it expired 09/30/2026, and reissuing it requires re-review) and F-1, the permanent second access. I will address those separately and call you Monday to walk through this memo.
______________________________
Max Braddock
Project Manager, Sundial Engineering & Survey

**What has to happen first:**
